# Decisions

Short record of choices that are expensive to reverse or easy to accidentally undo.

---

## 1. One renderer. The calendar is generated by Python only.

**Decided:** August 2026
**Status:** Active

### What

`python/build.py` is the only thing that renders the calendar. There is no second
implementation, in any language.

The Next.js web app that lived in `src/` was removed from `main` and preserved on the
branch **`web-ui-parked`**.

### Why

The web app reimplemented the calendar from scratch — its own cell logic, its own
Important Dates builder, its own PDF renderer (`@react-pdf` alongside WeasyPrint). The
two implementations were never checked against each other, and they drifted:

| | Python | Web app |
|---|---|---|
| Important Dates entries from `all_events.csv` | 45 | 56 |
| `no_school` days built from the same 14 CSV rows | 14 | 20 |

The 20 was a real bug. The web app's type table mapped `grades_due` to `no_school`, so
five ordinary school days rendered as black "No School" cells — 2025-11-12, 2026-01-21,
2026-02-02, 2026-04-10 and 2026-06-10. Nothing caught it, because nothing compared the
two outputs.

The consolidation gap was smaller but the same shape: Python groups repeat events under
one heading (`10/23, 2/19, 4/23, 6/4  PTSA: Board Meeting`), the web app printed four
separate lines. The asterisk rules had drifted too.

Two renderers of one document will always drift. Only one of them is printed and sent
home with families, so the other is a liability with no upside.

### If a web UI comes back

It very likely will — browser editing is genuinely useful for board members who won't
touch a CSV. When it does:

> **The web app edits `data/all_events.csv`. It does not render the calendar.**

Give it a preview if you like, but the artifact that gets printed comes from
`build.py`. The moment a second thing knows how to draw a day cell, this problem is back.

The parked branch is a reference for the UI work, not a starting point to merge — it
carries the duplicate renderer and an unauthenticated write API.

---

## 2. Unknown event types fail the build. The renderer never guesses.

**Decided:** August 2026
**Status:** Active

### What

Every event type is declared once, in the registry in `python/calendar_gen/event_types.py`. A type in
the CSV that isn't in the registry is a **validation error naming the row** — not a
default, not a silent skip.

### Why

This is the class of bug that produced the black school days above. The old code did:

```python
TYPE_NORMALIZATION.get(raw_type, raw_type)     # Python: silently passes through
TYPE_NORMALIZATION[normalized] || null          # TypeScript: silently guessed no_school
```

Both were guesses. One was wrong in a way that misinformed families.

### What this does *not* mean

The renderer has no opinion about **which** dates belong on the calendar. If a row is in
the CSV, it appears. That's the author's call, not the tool's.

The registry only declares **how** each type is drawn. To put a new kind of date on the
calendar, add it to the registry and say what it looks like — a one-line change, and now
it's a deliberate choice rather than an accident of what some lookup happened to return.

Types that should be listed in Important Dates but shouldn't change how the school day
looks set no `fill` and no `circle` — see `informational` in the registry, which
is what `grades_due` uses.

---

## 3. The editor edits data. It does not draw.

`web/` puts a form in front of `data/all_events.csv` so that a PTSA volunteer can
move a date without a terminal. It is the second web app this repository has had, and
the first one is the reason for decision #1 — so the shape of this one was chosen to
make the same failure impossible rather than merely discouraged.

### What went wrong last time

Two implementations of "draw the calendar" drifted. The TypeScript one guessed
`no_school` for a type it did not recognise, and five ordinary school days went home to
families marked as no school.

### Why a form is not a second renderer

The editor never answers a question about the calendar itself. Every such question is
delegated, and there is nowhere else for the answer to come from:

| Question | Answered by |
|---|---|
| What kinds of date are there? | `event_types.choices()` — the registry |
| Is this set of dates valid? | `calendar_gen.pipeline` |
| What does the page look like? | `calendar_gen.pipeline`, rendered |
| Does it still fit on one page? | `Build.publish_problems()` |
| What gets published? | the deploy workflow, unchanged |

`pipeline.py` was extracted for this. Those rules previously lived inside `build.py`'s
`main()`, reachable only by running the script, so an editor would have had to
reimplement them — and a second *validator* fails the same way as a second renderer
while being much harder to notice. Nothing looks wrong until the day somebody publishes
a blank page.

The line to hold, when adding to `web/`: **if you are writing a rule about dates or
about drawing, you are in the wrong file.**

### Git as the database

There is no database. The dates are already a CSV under version control, so a second
copy in Postgres would mean two answers to "what are this year's dates?" and a migration
to get them back out. Git already provides history, authorship, diffs and revert, which
is the entire feature list that was asked for.

It also decides what happens when this app dies. A volunteer-run tool should be
survivable: if the editor stops working in three years, the dates are still a CSV in a
repository that `build.py` still renders, and they can still be edited on GitHub.

The same reasoning keeps publishing on the existing workflow. The editor pushes to
`main` and stops there. Building a PDF itself would have made it a second publisher —
faster, and eventually disagreeing with the first.

### The password

One shared password, not accounts. Board members change every year, and per-person
accounts need a person to administer them who is also a volunteer. The first time
nobody does it, either someone who should be able to fix a date cannot, or an account
that should have gone stays live.

What makes that safe enough is not the password. It is that every change is committed,
attributed and revertible in seconds, that publishing is a separate deliberate press,
and that the worst case is a school calendar that is briefly wrong.
